[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in maths an expression has no effects, so i = i++ and x = ++i look like statements about equal quantities. In Java ++ changes i as soon as it is evaluated, and the expression's value (old or new) is then used by the rest of the expression.
[1] misconception (M) -> PostIncrementAssignsLater: wrong rule: i = i++ increases i by 1. Right rule: i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> PostIncrementAssignsLater: Applies left-to-right evaluation (LT) unevenly: lets an increment happen 'at the end of the statement' in one place but immediately in another. (here mixing in: "i = i++ increases i by 1")
[3] misconception (M) -> PrePostIncrementSameValue: wrong rule: x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x. Right rule: Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.

[0] names_the_element (N): A side effect is a change to a variable's value made while evaluating an expression, e.g. by ++, -- or an assignment used inside a larger expression.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Java evaluates the left operand of a binary operator fully before the right, and all operands (except &&, ||, ?:) before the operation; ++i yields the new value and i++ the old one.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Evaluate operands left to right, applying each side effect at the moment its operand is evaluated; then apply the operator; for an assignment, the right side's value is stored last.
[1] output_prediction (OP): With i = 5: i = i++ leaves 5 (old value stored back after the increment); x = i++ + i gives 5 + 6 = 11; j += j++ with j = 1 gives 2.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One evaluation of i++ changes i by 1 and returns the old value; a later assignment in the same statement can overwrite that change.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The result of an expression with a side effect depends on the value the increment expression evaluates to: old for i++, new for ++i.
[1] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: avoid it - write each change as its own statement (x = i; i++;) so the order of effects is visible; the book avoids statements like x = ++i.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> PostIncrementAssignsLater: Splitting x = i++; into x = i; i++; preserves behaviour; splitting it into i++; x = i; changes x by 1. Reordering the operands of an expression that contains a side effect can change the result.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Rely on side-effect order only when reading other people's code; in your own code keep at most one side effect per statement and never read and modify the same variable in one expression.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: i++ yields the old value; assigning it back undoes the increment. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: i = i++ (or j = j++) used as an update: the variable never changes.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Pre- and post-increment yield different values. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Using x = ++i where x = i++ was meant (or vice versa): x is off by one.
